1.note: Yahweh is speaking of the city of Jerusalem as if she were a woman, a barren woman who has never given birth. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you who are like a barren woman]

The implied “you” in the imperatives **Sing joyfully**, **break forth**, and **cry aloud** is feminine singular because it refers to Zion, which is being personified as a woman. For the same reason, the words “you” and “your” and the implied “you” in imperatives are feminine singular in the rest of this chapter. So use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction, and use the feminine form if your language marks that distinction.

Yahweh is speaking of the future people of Jerusalem as if they were **the sons of the one being desolate**, a deserted woman, and he speaks of a woman who has a husband as **the married**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the people of Jerusalem when it was deserted will be more numerous than its people when it was populated]

Isaiah is using the adjective **married** as a noun to mean a certain kind of woman. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the woman who is married]

2.note: Yahweh is speaking of the increase of Jerusalem’s people as if the city were a tent that needed to be enlarged, telling it to **Broaden the place of your tent**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Make the space of your tent larger]

Yahweh is using the pronoun **they** in a general sense, not to refer to specific people. Use an expression for this that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [may people stretch out]

3.note: Yahweh is referring to all directions by naming two extremes, **the right** and **the left**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in all directions]

Yahweh is speaking of the descendants of Jerusalem as if they were **seed** that she would produce. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and your descendants]

The expression **desolated** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and they will make people inhabit cities that had become desolate]

4.q: אַל־תִּֽירְאִי֙ כִּי־לֹ֣א תֵב֔וֹשִׁי וְ⁠אַל־תִּכָּלְמִ֖י כִּ֣י לֹ֣א תַחְפִּ֑ירִי
4.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [You will not be ashamed or humiliated ever again]

4.q: אַל־תִּֽירְאִי֙ כִּי־לֹ֣א תֵב֔וֹשִׁי וְ⁠אַל־תִּכָּלְמִ֖י & לֹ֣א תַחְפִּ֑ירִי כִּ֣י
4.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **shame** and **disgrace**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [May you not fear, for you will not be ashamed, and may you not be humiliated, for you will not be disgraced]

For poetic purposes, Isaiah is using two different words that have basically the same meaning. The ULT translates each one as **shame** because English does not have two different words that it can use in this context. But if your language does, it would be appropriate to use them here.

The expression **be humiliated** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and may no one humiliate you]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **shame**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how you were shamed when you were young]

4.q: כִּ֣י & בֹ֤שֶׁת עֲלוּמַ֨יִ⁠ךְ֙ תִּשְׁכָּ֔חִי וְ⁠חֶרְפַּ֥ת אַלְמְנוּתַ֖יִ⁠ךְ לֹ֥א תִזְכְּרִי־עֽוֹד
4.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [For you will completely forget the shame you felt when you were young and widowed]

The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]

Yahweh is speaking of the time when he abandoned Jerusalem as if it were a woman’s **widowhood**, when her husband had died. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you will not remember the disgrace of when I abandoned you]

5.note: Isaiah is speaking of Yahweh, the one who made Jerusalem, as if he were her **husband**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your Maker will care for you like a husband]

The expression **he is called** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people call him]

6.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **a wife abandoned and grieved of spirit** is distressed and full of sorrow, so are **you**, the people of Jerusalem, whom Yahweh has called back to himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as distressed as a wife who has been abandoned and is full of sorrow]

The expression **abandoned** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [like a wife whose husband has abandoned her, one grieved of spirit]

Isaiah is using **a wife of youth** as a common expression of the culture to mean “a woman whom a man married when she was young.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and a woman married in her youth]

Isaiah is not using this possessive form **your God** to indicate that the people of Jerusalem possess or control Yahweh. Rather Isaiah is using these words to indicate that Yahweh is the God whom the people of Jerusalem worship. Alternate translation: [the God whom you worship]

7.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **compassions**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [but because I am very compassionate,]

8.note: Yahweh is speaking of his anger as if it were a **flood** that overwhelmed everything. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [In overwhelming anger]

Here, **my face** represents Yahweh’s presence and favor toward his people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I removed myself] or [I turned away my favor]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [but because I will always be faithful to my covenant,] of [but because I will be eternally faithful to my covenant,]

Isaiah uses the word **but** here to indicate a contrast between Yahweh hiding his face in anger for a moment and Yahweh showing compassion because of his covenant faithfulness that lasts forever. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [however, because of my everlasting covenant faithfulness]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **compassion**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [I will be compassionate toward you]

9.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because this situation is like the waters of Noah to me]

Yahweh is speaking of the present time as if it were **the waters of Noah**, the time of the great flood. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [this situation is like the time of Noah’s flood for me]

9.q: נִשְׁבַּ֗עְתִּי מֵ⁠עֲבֹ֥ר מֵי־נֹ֛חַ ע֖וֹד עַל־הָ⁠אָ֑רֶץ כֵּ֥ן נִשְׁבַּ֛עְתִּי & מִ⁠קְּצֹ֥ף עָלַ֖יִ⁠ךְ וּ⁠מִ⁠גְּעָר־בָּֽ⁠ךְ
9.note: Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb **swore** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [I solemnly swore that the waters of Noah would not pass over the earth again; so I solemnly swear that I will not be angry with you and will not rebuke you]

10.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]

10.q: כִּ֤י הֶֽ⁠הָרִים֙ יָמ֔וּשׁוּ וְ⁠הַ⁠גְּבָע֖וֹת תְּמוּטֶ֑נָה וְ⁠חַסְדִּ֞⁠י מֵ⁠אִתֵּ֣⁠ךְ לֹֽא יָמ֗וּשׁ וּ⁠בְרִ֤ית שְׁלוֹמִ⁠י֙ לֹ֣א תָמ֔וּט אָמַ֥ר מְרַחֲמֵ֖⁠ךְ יְהוָֽה
10.note: Yahweh uses the word **but** here to indicate a contrast between what may happen to the mountains and hills and what will happen to his covenant faithfulness. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Even though the mountains may depart, and the hills may shake, my covenant faithfulness will not depart from you, and the covenant of my peace will not shake,” says Yahweh, the one having compassion on you] or [For the mountains may depart, and the hills may shake. Nevertheless, my covenant faithfulness will not depart from you, and the covenant of my peace will not shake,” says Yahweh, the one having compassion on you]

Yahweh is speaking of **the mountains** and **the hills** as if they were living things that could depart and shake on their own. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the mountains may be destroyed, and the hills may crumble]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [but my being faithful to my covenant]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and the covenant in which I promise that you will be safe and well]

11.note: Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [You who are poor, tempested, and not comforted]

Yahweh is using the adjective **Poor** as a noun to mean a certain kind of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [You poor ones]

Yahweh is speaking of the people of Jerusalem as if they were **tempested**, meaning that they have been tossed about by a violent storm. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [afflicted by enemies]

The expression **tempested** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Storms have battered you poor ones]

The expression **not comforted** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [whom no one comforts]

11.q: אָנֹכִ֜י מַרְבִּ֤יץ בַּ⁠פּוּךְ֙ אֲבָנַ֔יִ⁠ךְ וִ⁠יסַדְתִּ֖י⁠ךְ בַּ⁠סַּפִּירִֽים
11.note: Yahweh is speaking of restoring the city of Jerusalem as if he were **setting your stones in antimony** and laying its foundations **with sapphires**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am going to rebuild you beautifully, with your stones laid as if in antimony and your foundations as precious as sapphires]

Here, **antimony** is a kind of dark mineral that was used as a setting for gemstones. If your readers would not be familiar with what antimony is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [in a dark mortar]

12.q: וְ⁠שַׂמְתִּ֤י כַּֽדְכֹד֙ שִׁמְשֹׁתַ֔יִ⁠ךְ וּ⁠שְׁעָרַ֖יִ⁠ךְ לְ⁠אַבְנֵ֣י אֶקְדָּ֑ח וְ⁠כָל גְּבוּלֵ֖⁠ךְ לְ⁠אַבְנֵי חֵֽפֶץ
12.note: Yahweh is speaking of the future splendor of Jerusalem as if he would rebuild its walls and gates out of precious stones, making its **battlements rubies** and its **gates into stones of beryl**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will make your city so glorious that it will be as if your battlements were rubies and your gates were beryl and all of your border were precious stones]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe **stones** that are characterized by **delight**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [into delightful stones]

13.note: Yahweh is speaking of the people who live in Jerusalem as if they were her **sons**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And all of your inhabitants]
Yahweh is using this possessive form to mean people whom he himself teaches. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [will be people whom Yahweh himself teaches]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [your sons’ lives will be very peaceful]

14.note: The expression **established** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I will establish you]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [as you live rightly]

The verb translated as **Be far** is an imperative, but it communicates a result rather than a command. If in this context an imperative would not communicate a result for your readers, then use a form in your language that would communicate a result. Alternate translation: [You will be far]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [you will not fear, and be far from terror]

Yahweh is speaking of **terror** as if it were a living thing that could come near to a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you will not experience it]

15.note: Yahweh is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Look]

Yahweh is using **will fall before you** as a common expression of the culture to mean “will be defeated by you.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [whoever quarrels with you will be defeated by you] or [you will defeat whoever quarrels with you]

16.note: Yahweh is speaking as if he wanted his listeners to actually see something, using the word **Behold** to focus their attention on the important statement that follows. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Listen] or [Pay attention]

Yahweh is not referring to a specific **craftsman**. He means craftsmen in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [craftsmen in general]

Yahweh is stating the pronoun **I** separately in each clause, even though the verb translated as **I have created** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that he alone is responsible for creating both the craftsman who makes weapons and the destroyer who destroys with them, contrasting the two things that he himself does. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [Indeed, I am the one who has created the craftsman blowing on a fire of coal and bringing out a weapon for its work, and indeed, I am the one who has created the destroyer to destroy]

Isaiah is using **bringing out** as a common expression of the culture to mean “producing” or “making.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [fashioning] or [making]

The pronoun **its** could refer to (1) the work of the weapon, in which case the phrase means the purpose for which the weapon is made. Alternate translation: [a weapon for its purpose] or (2) the work of the craftsman, in which case the phrase refers to the work that the craftsman does. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [a weapon made by his work]

For poetic purposes, Isaiah is using two different words that have basically the same meaning. The ULT translates them as **destroyer** and **destroy** because English does not have two different words that it can use in this context. But if your language does, it would be appropriate to use them here.

17.note: Here, **weapon** represents an attack that someone makes against a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Every attack made against you]

The expression **formed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Every weapon that anyone forms against you]

Here, **tongue** represents an accusation that someone speaks against another person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and every accusation raised against you in judgment]

Yahweh is speaking of what he gives to his servants as if it were an **inheritance** that they receive from a parent. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [is what Yahweh gives to his servants]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **inheritance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [is what I give to the servants of Yahweh]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and I am the one who vindicates them]
